questions.prompt: With N = 1496 counts per wheel turn and a speed estimate from the counts of one 10 ms period, what is the speed quantum in rad/s?

questions.prompt: A uint16_t counter reads 65500 and then 40. The correct signed delta is:
options: -65460, because the counter simply went down by that many counts.
+65460, because the wheel must have turned forward a long way.
0, because a jump this large is an invalid sample and is discarded.
questions.explanation: Modular subtraction maps the difference into the signed range: +76.

questions.prompt: A parser receives 50 bytes of garbage and then a valid stuffed frame. Which design lets it recover?
options: Each delimiter byte 0x7E discards the partial buffer and starts a new frame, which is then validated by length and CRC.
The parser must be restarted by the host after every CRC failure, since it cannot recover alone.
The parser waits until it has received exactly 12 bytes and then validates them wherever they started, which is simple to implement.
The parser keeps all garbage and tries every offset when the CRC fails, until some offset passes.
questions.explanation: Delimiter-based resynchronisation bounds the damage of garbage to one frame.

questions.prompt: A 26-byte worst-case wire frame is sent at 100 Hz over 115200 baud. What is the worst-case link load in percent?
With Ki = 1.5 and a 6 rad/s error held for 1 s, the integrator reaches 9.0 without anti-windup. What does that number mean?
options: The integrator will settle to 9.0, which is the correct duty for 6 rad/s at steady state.
Nine times the full duty range is stored, so the output stays saturated long after the wheel is released.
The loop gain is 9, so the loop is unstable and Kp has to be reduced by that factor.
The wheel will run at 9 rad/s after release, which is the steady-state speed of the loop.
questions.explanation: The stored integral is far outside the output range [-1, 1]; unwinding it takes a long time.

questions.prompt: What should the PWM output be right after the firmware boots, before any command has arrived?
options: The last speed stored in flash, so the robot resumes the task it was doing before the reset.
A small creep duty so the encoders can be checked immediately, then zero when a command arrives.
Zero: the watchdog starts in the expired state and is only armed by the first valid command.
Undefined until the first frame: the pins are left floating so the driver chip decides its own default.
questions.explanation: Safe defaults: outputs are zero at boot and whenever data is stale.

questions.prompt: A robot drives at 0.4 m/s and the watchdog timeout is 80 ms. How far (in cm) does it travel before the PWM is cut, ignoring coasting?
With the radius already corrected, a robot with b_est = 0.150 m spins 5 true turns (1800 degrees) and odometry reports 1930 degrees. What is the new track width in metres?
A step to 6.0 rad/s peaks at 6.4 rad/s. What is the overshoot in percent of the target?
Why does the CAP02 log compute omega over a 50 ms window instead of one 10 ms period?
options: Because the motor needs 50 ms to respond, so shorter windows would show the wrong speed.
One 10 ms period has a 0.42 rad/s quantum (7 % of 6 rad/s); 50 ms gives 0.084 rad/s, so the spec can be checked at 2 %.
Because the CRC check needs five frames before the counts are valid enough to use, as the parser buffers them.
Because the decoder only updates the count every 50 ms in the simulator.
questions.explanation: Count quantisation limits what a short window can show.

questions.prompt: Build a worst-case latency budget for the spec 'command to first response within 20 ms' with a 100 Hz firmware loop and a 115200-baud link.
rubric: Lists the three terms: wait for the next 10 ms tick, link time of the 14-byte frame (about 1.2 ms), and time for the first count (about 7 ms).
Adds them (about 18 ms) and compares with 20 ms, noting how little margin remains.
Names one thing that breaks the budget (USB-serial latency timers, extra buffering) and what to do about it.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Write a test plan for the frame parser: exhaustive bit flips, resynchronisation after garbage, and a long clean run.
rubric: Builds a valid frame with a known CRC (check value 0xF4 for the string 123456789) and flips every one of its 96 bits, expecting rejection.
Feeds 50 random garbage bytes (seeded) before a valid stuffed frame and expects exactly one frame out, and includes a frame whose body contains 0x7E and 0x7D.
Runs 10 000 clean frames expecting zero loss and checks the link load figure against the 50 % limit.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Explain why the speed loop is written in portable C and called from the simulator through ctypes, instead of being written in Python. Name two risks of this choice.
rubric: Says that integer widths, wrap-around, timing and buffer limits are exactly the bugs that appear on an MCU, and that the same sources can be flashed to an ESP32.
Names a risk such as float versus double differences between host and MCU, or ctypes silently assuming int argument types.
Names a second risk such as the simulator tick not reproducing interrupt timing or the toolchain (gcc, cmake) not being installed.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
